Here's a short history.

  • Linux was invented in the early 90s and was pretty difficult to use until the early 2000s. There were many distributions, but none were approachable for non-technical users.
  • Mark Cuban, flush from successful IT investments, decided to commission a Linux distribution targeted at non-technical users. He named it Ubuntu.
  • Ubuntu got most of the usability right, but it was still missing details like fancy fonts, browser plugins, etc., which the user had to manually install.
  • Another project called Linux Mint started up, based on Ubuntu, but making up for these omissions.
  • As time went on, the Ubuntu project lost its way even further, putting ads in its user interface and switching to a counterintuitive window manager. Linux Mint always put users first.
  • This is why you'll hear it recommended above most other distributions.

First thing you need to do if you're going to switch is back up your files. This can be done by burning dvd's, or copying all your stuff to an external drive, formatted FAT32 so it can be read and written by Windows or Linux (FAT32 supports individual file size up to 4GB).

if i switch over to Linux, what happens to the old software on it.

If you dual boot then you can choose to keep your old OS (and programs/files), so each time you turn it on you choose Windows or Linux, so in that case you would still have your old stuff in Windows, but it would be unavailable when booted into Linux. If you choose to wipe everything and just use Linux, then all the Windows programs/files will be gone, but Linux comes with Firefox (&Chrome), VLC, and office & common stuff that the average person would need.

Don't count on your files surviving a Linux install, back them all up to disks or an external drive to be safe, for seriously.

The nuts and bolts of making your system boot in to linux is a google search away. It's basically just switching the boot order in your bios so your dvd or usb drive gets checked for a bootable OS before your harddrive does. burn the Linux dvd as an iso/image, not just as data, or Google how to make a bootable USB thumb drive.
